title: The Quiet Question at Harbour Workshop
author: ONE HOME original short-reader collection
pages: Ellis arrived at Harbour Workshop before the afternoon activity began. The room was quiet, but there was plenty to prepare. On a small table lay a pencil, ready to be used. Then the organiser explained the difficulty: two posters gave different opening times. Ellis had expected a simple afternoon and felt uncertain. Instead of pretending to know the answer, Ellis asked for a few minutes to look carefully. There was still time to understand what had happened before anyone made a decision.

The first step was to check the date and ask the organiser which notice was current. This took longer than making a quick guess, but it gave the group something useful to work with. Ellis wrote down what was known and put a question mark beside what still needed checking. A friend suggested rushing ahead. “If we get the first part wrong, we may have to do everything twice,” Ellis replied. Together they compared the information. One detail mattered more than the others: a plan had to work for the people who would actually use it.

Soon the group had a possible answer. They could replace the old poster with a clear new notice. Ellis explained the idea, then asked the others what might go wrong. At first, nobody spoke. After a moment, a younger visitor raised a concern. The group listened rather than dismissing it. They changed a small part of the plan and tried it on a limited scale. The trial was not perfect, but it showed them what to improve. Ellis used a pencil to keep track of the next step.

When the visitors arrived, the group put the revised plan into practice. Someone who had missed the discussion asked why they had chosen this approach. Ellis explained both the problem and the reason for the decision. That explanation helped the newcomer take part without feeling left behind. During the afternoon, the team checked how things were going. They did not assume that silence meant success. They asked people directly and made another small adjustment when it was needed.

By the end of the afternoon, Harbour Workshop felt different. The original problem had become a chance to practise being thoughtful. Ellis returned a pencil to the table and wrote a note for the next group: “Check, listen, try, then improve.” The organiser thanked everyone, including the visitor whose question had changed the plan. Ellis was pleased, but the best part was knowing how the group had reached its answer. They had not needed one person to know everything. They had needed people who were willing to think together.

choices: two posters gave different opening times
two groups wanted to use the same space
new visitors found the entrance difficult to locate
a box of donated objects had lost its labels

questions.prompt: What did the group decide to do?
choices: agree a timetable that gave each group a turn
replace the old poster with a clear new notice
add simple signs at the confusing turning points
write labels that explained where each object came from

questions.prompt: Why did the group test a small version first?
choices: To discover problems before using the full plan
To make the task last forever
